papers.title: A red fluorescent sensor for intensity-and lifetime imaging of cAMP in living cells
papers.abstract: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) is a crucial intracellular messenger involved in neuromodulation and plasticity, but more information on its spatiotemporal regulation is desirable. Here we constructed a red fluorescent indicator based on a truncated cAMP binding site derived from a regulatory PKA subunit of protozoan origin. It contains a single binding site for cAMP highly specific for cAMP over cGMP. chILI (cAMP highly-responsive Intensity and Lifetime Indicator) can be imaged as an intensity-based probe, but alternatively also offers options for fluorescence lifetime imaging. When expressed in the mouse brain using AAV-vector mediated gene transfer, it reports spontaneous and evoked cAMP transients from CA1 neurons in the hippocampus of awake mice. chILI will add valuable options for monitoring cAMP in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Naturalistic recall preserves temporal specificity despite cortical feature reorganization
papers.abstract: Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock. A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.

papers.title: Unilateral naris occlusion with custom-made plugs for reversible olfactory deprivation in juvenile and adult mice
papers.abstract: Deprivation paradigms that reduce environmental input have been successfully applied across multiple species and sensory modalities, including vision, audition, somatosensation, and olfaction in order to understand how neurons and circuits respond to loss of sensory input. One notable advantage of studying sensory deprivation in the rodent olfactory system is the ease and control with which smell loss can be induced. Various methods of olfactory deprivation have long been available and rely on blocking a nostril, either through invasive and often non-reversible approaches such as chemical ablation or surgical procedures, or through reversible approaches such as unilateral naris occlusion using custom-made nose plugs. Here, we provide a systematic description of this well-established method, including its construction from commercially available materials, procedures, validation, and reliability in post-weaning mice, thereby providing a detailed and reproducible framework for controlled, reversible olfactory deprivation.

papers.title: Locomotor activity enhances environmental representation by boosting visuo-frontal communication
papers.abstract: During environment exploration we rapidly acquire visual information to identify targets of interest. Here, we discovered that locomotion limits how long natural scenes are viewed dur- ing free exploration. Whether the brain has developed compensatory mechanisms to ensure that sensory information is accurately transmitted to downstream areas during and after locomotion is unknown. We examined this issue by recording the spiking activity of popula- tions of neurons in visual and prefrontal cortex in conjunction with wireless recordings of oculomotor events while macaques moved freely to explore their environment or performed treadmill bipedal locomotion. The communication between visuo-frontal cortical areas was enhanced during and after locomotion to increase visual-evoked responses and population coding accuracy in prefrontal, but not visual cortical neurons. This in turn improved behav- ioral performance in a freely moving visual detection task after locomotion. Electrical stim- ulation further revealed elevated inter-areal synaptic efficacy during locomotor activity. The mechanism whereby locomotion enhances stimulus coding accuracy in prefrontal cortex and behavioral performance by increasing visuo-frontal communication is functionally beneficial during environmental exploration when incoming stimuli are rapidly changing and the win- dow for perceptual decisions is temporally restricted.

papers.title: An Eyewear-Based EEG Interface for Temporal-Region Monitoring and Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) devices are often impractical for ambulatory settings due to their reliance on specialized hardware and expert operation. To address this, we developed a user-friendly eyewear-based EEG system featuring dry titanium electrodes positioned approximately 5 mm inferoposterior to the T7/T8 sites (near the ears), with metal nose pads serving as references. We evaluated the system across 103 recordings spanning five paradigms: alpha reactivity, blink-related transients, fatigue, attention, and video-elicited emotion. Following quality control, 93.2-100.0% of epochs were retained. The system demonstrated high sensitivity to ocular transients, showing significant amplitude increases during the blinking task. The emotion task yielded the most robust state-related features, with statistically significant differences in differential entropy across negative, neutral, and positive video categories, achieving balanced accuracies of 0.882 for two-class and 0.667 for three-class prediction. Despite challenges at the multiple testing correction stage, the alpha reactivity and fatigue contrast tasks were still noteworthy to some extent. The attention paradigm revealed a consistent increase in differential entropy during focused states, and the eyewear system outperformed the Muse headband in group-held-out classification. These findings provide strong evidence for the feasibility of temporal-region eyewear EEG acquisition, highlighting its potential applications in the real-world, particularly for emotion recognition.

papers.title: Monoaminergic changes are associated with impaired neurogenesis along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus in ageing and dementia
papers.abstract: Neurogenesis persists in the adult human hippocampus and is thought to support memory and emotional regulation. Both normal ageing and Parkinson disease dementia (PDD) are associated with reduced hippocampal neurogenesis, but why this occurs and how this might change across the across the hippocampal axis remains unclear. Here, we quantified the expression of genes regulating neurogenesis from stem cell production to neuron maturation and examined their relationship with monoaminergic activity throughout the post-mortem hippocampus in young and aged individuals, as well as in individuals with PDD. DCX and MKI67 expression were markedly reduced in PDD cases throughout the hippocampus, while GFAP and GFAP{delta} were elevated in aged control individuals but not in PDD. Dopamine and serotonin levels were unchanged but reduced levels of the dopamine metabolite DOPAC, and increased levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA, were present across the hippocampal axis in PDD. Hierarchical regression analysis identified DOPAC and 5-HIAA as significant predictors of DCX and MKI67 expression independent of diagnostic group. Coupling between stem cell markers and proliferative output was preserved in the hippocampus of young controls but was absent in aged controls and in PDD. These data suggest changes in monoaminergic systems are linked to stage-specific deficits in neuronal proliferation and maturation, identifying a potential mechanistic bridge to cognitive decline in PDD.

papers.title: Inosine Triphosphate Pyrophosphatase as a Candidate Associated with White Matter Abnormalities in Chronic Heart Failure
papers.abstract: Background: White matter hyperintensities (WMHs) are common with normal brain aging and frequently observed also in chronic heart failure (CHF). However, the relationship between CHF and white matter abnormalities and the biological factors remain unclear. We investigated WMH and associated white matter microstructural changes, such as fractional anisotropy (FA), in CHF and explored candidate molecular factors. Methods: We conducted a longitudinal prospective observation including brain T2-FLAIR magnetic resonace imaging for 32 asymptomatic Stage B (mean age 63.3{+/-}10.5 years; 25% women) and 23 symptomatic Stage C CHF patients (mean age 67.3{+/-}7.1 years; 30% women). Plasma proteomics and Mendelian randomization (MR) were used to identify candidate proteins associated with both CHF and WMH. The association of candidate proteins was further investigated using complementary analyses in CHF rats, cultured cortical neurons, and community-based genetic data in UK Biobank. Results: Global WMH volume increased more in Stage C than Stage B patients, predominantly near the anterior periventricular white matter, despite comparable cardiac indices (4,717{+/-}5,335 mm3 vs. 2,116{+/-}3,134 mm3, P=0.027). SomaScan-based proteomic analysis of plasma samples from this patient cohort revealed that 44 proteins are significantly associated with both Stage C CHF and WMH progression (P<0.05). Of these 44 proteins, two-step Mendelian randomization analysis identified inosine triphosphate pyrophosphatase (ITPA) as the only candidate protein, further supported by an association between rare variants in ITPA and FA. In CHF rats, the anterior pericallosal cortex showed decreases in myelin basic protein density and FA and an increase in ITPA expression compared to sham rats. In cultured cortical neurons, recombinant ITPA exposure reduced total axonal length. Conclusions: Symptomatic CHF was associated with WMH and impaired white matter integrity. ITPA emerged as a candidate factor across human, animal, and cellular analyses. These findings provide a basis for investgating the biological pathways linking CHF and white matter injury.

papers.title: Disentangling visual and motor contributions to continuous psychophysics
papers.abstract: Continuous psychophysics measures visual function by asking observers to track a randomly moving target. Because continuous responses provide more information than traditional discrete judgements, a few minutes of tracking can estimate visual sensitivity, making the approach attractive for testing children and patients. Tracking performance is often summarized by cross-correlating the target and cursor velocities: the resulting cross-correlogram peak, lag and width index how strongly, quickly and sharply the observer responds to the target. Tracking, however, requires both seeing the target and moving the cursor towards it, so poor tracking may reflect impaired vision, impaired motor control, or both. Here, we test whether visual and motor contributions to tracking performance can be told apart. Participants tracked a target with a computer mouse while wearing glasses that simulate two levels of visual impairment, using either their dominant or their non-dominant hand. We find that both manipulations alter the cross-correlogram metrics, lowering the peak correlation and delaying and broadening the response, but in different proportions. Visual impairment mainly delays and broadens the response, and does so in proportion to each participant's loss of visual acuity. The non-dominant hand mainly lowers the peak correlation. Two signatures of motor control explain this difference: with the non-dominant hand, participants pause more often and for longer, and move more noisily between pauses, whereas visual impairment alters neither. Together, response lag, time paused and movement noise reveal whether a change in tracking is visual or motor in almost every participant. Our findings demonstrate that, given a baseline measurement, the same tracking data that measure vision can also reveal whether a change in performance reflects a change in what an individual sees or in how they move.

papers.title: Loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment across social and nonsocial contexts
papers.abstract: Loneliness is associated with cognitive biases that diverge from normative patterns of understanding and may be reflected in altered neural responses to the world. Here, we examined how loneliness modulates neural synchrony across individuals during the processing of social and nonsocial information. Using high-resolution movie-watching fMRI data (n = 178) from the Human Connectome Project, we applied intersubject correlation analyses to identify context-dependent neural signature of loneliness. Lonely individuals primarily showed more idiosyncratic responses in regions within the default mode network, visual association cortex, and amygdala during social contexts, and in reward-related circuitry during nonsocial contexts. This suggests less stereotyped processing of social information and reward in lonely individuals. In contrast, lonely individuals exhibited greater neural synchrony in the nucleus accumbens during social contexts and in somatomotor regions during nonsocial contexts. This potentially reflects shared experiences of social craving and engagement with a socially irrelevant physical environment. These effects were robust against demographic similarities, kinship, depression, and objective levels of social connection. Together, these findings identify loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment, which may contribute to shaping how individuals process and interpret different aspects of the world.

papers.title: Disrupted mannosidase enzymes in C9orf72 ALS/FTD
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder resulting from the loss of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. Neuroinflammation, induced by glial cells including microglia (MG) and astrocytes, is an acknowledged aspect of this neurodegeneration. Generating induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neuroinflammatory models of ALS may help elucidate non-neuronal mechanisms of disease. Here, we analyze human postmortem tissue and an iPSC derived glia-crosstalk model identifying a reduction in Golgi enzymes MAN1A1 and MAN1A2 in addition to other glycan enzymes from ALS-associated microglia and astrocytes. Impaired Golgi and glycan metabolism is linked to inflammation and other related ALS disease mechanisms including impaired lysosomal proteostasis, altered extracellular matrix, disrupted secretion, and altered cell-cell signaling.

papers.title: Context-dependent effects of ketamine on emotional evidence integration
papers.abstract: Understanding others' emotions requires continuously integrating noisy affective information as emotional states change over time. Research on emotion processing, however, has thus far focused on static environments or discrete events. Here, we developed a continuous emotional evidence integration task in which participants had to track the average emotional state in a rapidly changing sequence of faces under different levels of environmental volatility. This allowed us to examine emotion integration in changing environments. In online (n=92) and in-person (n=29) cohorts, participants integrated emotional information over longer timescales in stable environments while relying more strongly on recent evidence under volatility, consistent with principles established in perceptual decision-making. We further examined whether this process was modulated by ketamine, an NMDA receptor antagonist associated with evidence integration in the perceptual domain. We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject study and probed emotion integration during the post-acute period, approximately 1.5 hours after the infusion. Ketamine modulated the temporal weighting of emotional evidence, shifting the balance between recent and past information depending on environmental volatility. Together, these findings show that emotional evidence integration dynamically adapts to the statistical structure of the environment and that ketamine can further modulate this process, which may have relevance for affective disorders.

papers.title: Amnesia Induced by Suppressing the Focus of Internal Attention
papers.abstract: Our thoughts can recede as we direct attention to the external world. This experience may reflect the suppression of thoughts about past events, future worries, or stray ideas that could otherwise disrupt focus. Such thoughts may arise spontaneously from replay mechanisms supported by the episodic memory system; hence, sustaining external focus may require suppressing these systems to stop internal distraction. Here, periods of high external focus disrupted diverse episodic content activated near in time, inducing an 'amnesic shadow'. This shadow occurred for both novel content and already formed memories and exhibited key markers of active suppression: forgetting beyond expectations from time alone, which generalised to an alternative reminder. External attention therefore automatically engages an active suppression mechanism that appears to broadly inhibit cognitive systems supporting the emergence of distracting thoughts. The findings raise the possibility that people may naturally gravitate toward activities demanding external attention, unwittingly, to regulate unwanted thoughts.

papers.title: Neural dynamics become significantly faster and more nonlinear at the peak of information processing
papers.abstract: The temporal scale at which neural populations preserve stimulus information is often treated as fixed, even though population activity changes rapidly during sensory processing. Whether the information-optimal scale changes within a single stimulus-evoked episode, and what determines its evolution, remains unclear. We developed Integration-Split, a decoding-based framework that estimates the time-varying temporal resolution of population spike trains. Across four visual paradigms and throughout the mouse visual hierarchy, the optimal scale contracted after stimulus onset and subsequently re-expanded. This pattern persisted across stimulus temporal frequencies and was largely absent in a hippocampal control. The optimal scale varied inversely with stimulus decodability, reaching its finest resolution when stimulus identity was most accurately decoded. Beyond this association, independently estimating the signal-noise autocorrelation balance across candidate window widths identified the window that maximized the autocorrelation-based signal-to-noise ratio, and this optimal width closely followed the Integration-Split trajectory. Consistent with these findings, stronger nonlinear predictive structure coincided with finer optimal temporal resolution, consistent with the idea that shorter integration windows are needed to preserve informative nonlinear population structure that would otherwise be attenuated by temporal averaging. To test the functional relevance of this organization, we trained a Transformer solely to decode stimulus identity, without providing the optimal temporal-scale pattern or Integration-Split outputs. Its learned attention exhibited a similar contraction-and-recovery profile, and disrupting heads with stronger correspondence produced larger decoding deficits. Together, these findings reveal a dynamically changing, information-optimal temporal scale in population coding, shaped by the evolving balance of signal and noise autocorrelation and by nonlinear population structure, and independently recapitulated in the learned attention of a Transformer trained without temporal-scale supervision.

papers.title: Connectome structure constrains neural activity across scales
papers.abstract: Connectomes can be represented at many resolutions, but coarse-graining risks discarding structure relevant to neural dynamics. Here we ask at what resolution a connectome preserves what it predicts about neural activity. In C. elegans, direct synaptic connectivity poorly predicts whether stimulating one neuron evokes a response in another. A parameter-free predictor based on paths through the connectome performs substantially better, with most predictive information carried by two-step paths and by the arrangement rather than the number of connections. Coarse-graining neurons into biological cell classes preserves these predictions despite discarding path structure, whereas random partitions degrade them. Connectivity alone identifies alternative coarse-grainings that preserve prediction down to about nine groups corresponding to nervous-system subsystems. Partitions inferred from newly hatched animals preserve adult predictions, and lineage-based partitions in Drosophila preserve path structure better than random coarse-graining. Functional prediction can therefore survive at resolutions far coarser than those required to preserve structure.

papers.title: Scn2a-deficient mice exhibit serotonergic dysfunction and altered behavioral responses to psilocybin
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prominent neurodevelopmental disorder affecting approximately 3.2% of children in the United States. Although ASD has traditionally been considered a polygenic disorder, advances in genetic testing have identified individual genes that can contribute to its development. Large-scale whole-exome sequencing has identified variants in SCN2A, which encodes the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2, as a leading monogenic cause of ASD. Social deficits are a core feature of ASD, and the serotonergic system has been implicated in the regulation of social behavior. Recent studies have demonstrated that serotonergic psychedelics, such as psilocybin, can increase sociability in mouse models of ASD. However, whether underlying genetic alterations associated with ASD influence behavioral responses to psilocybin remains poorly understood. Therefore, we investigated how Scn2a deficiency affects behavioral responses to psilocybin and whether these differences are accompanied by alterations in the serotonergic system. We found that Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited differential responses to psilocybin compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Specifically, psilocybin increased sociability in Scn2a-deficient mice without affecting anxiety-like behavior, whereas WT mice exhibited decreased anxiety-like behavior without increased sociability. Further behavioral evaluation revealed a reduced head twitch response in Scn2a-deficient mice following psilocybin administration compared to WT mice. To further investigate these differences, we examined serotonin levels and receptor expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a brain region implicated in social behavior and psychedelic action. Although baseline serotonin levels in the mPFC did not differ between genotypes, Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited altered serotonin receptor expression. We further characterized the serotonergic system by evaluating neuronal activity in the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus, a major source of serotonergic projections to the mPFC, and found increased spontaneous firing in Scn2a-deficient mice. Together, these findings highlight serotonergic alterations associated with SCN2A deficiency and the potential for serotonergic interventions to alleviate social deficits associated with SCN2A-related ASD.

papers.title: Contributions of Site Heterogeneity in Multi-site Brain-Phenotype Predictions
papers.abstract: Machine learning studies of brain-phenotype associations typically summarize accuracy with a single Pearson correlation, yet in harmonized multi-site data this metric is shaped by training-set size, feature and outcome variability, and true effect heterogeneity. We analyzed structural MRI data from the Reproducible Brain Charts consortium. After preprocessing and quality control, 3486 participants from 9 sites were retained. Three training set compositions were used to understand contributions of site heterogeneity after harmonization: within-site (Local), size-downsampled multi-site (Multi-Down), and full multi-site (Multi-Full). Another site-agnostic strategy (Overall) pooled all sites into a single dataset. All strategies included the target site in the training and testing samples. These analyses separate the contribution of the site effect from that of sample size. Between-site heterogeneity was extensive (age I^2 {approx} 95%). The overall correlation of age prediction (r = 0.73) exceeded the within-site meta-analytic estimate (Multi-Full r = 0.63). The improvement of correlation in the pooled dataset was driven by a mechanical inflation from the larger outcome variance. At matched sample size, within-site training outperformed harmonized multi-site training. Increasing the multi-site training sample size did not yield a significant advantage over within-site training. The apparent advantage of cross-dataset training thus appears to reflect training-set size rather than a benefit of multi-site composition per se. The same pattern generally held for the weaker brain-p-factor signals. Together, these results indicate that between-site heterogeneity in machine learning brain-phenotype prediction persists after harmonization. We recommend reporting site-level prediction accuracy and feature dispersion and standard deviation of the outcome variable alongside any pooled estimate to improve inter-site and inter-study comparison of machine learning prediction accuracy.

papers.title: The behaviour bends, the code holds: working-memory category information in the multiple-demand network across graded interruption
papers.abstract: Protecting working memory (WM) from interference is essential for goal-directed behaviour, yet its neural mechanisms remain unclear. The multiple-demand (MD) network - a set of frontoparietal regions recruited by diverse cognitive demands - is a candidate system for maintaining WM content under interference. We examined how the MD network represents a memorandum when an unrelated task interrupts maintenance. Participants memorised an image of a tool or animal and, during the delay, performed a digit task whose difficulty was parametrically varied (passive, easy, hard), allowing us to test how task engagement and associated cognitive demands affected concurrently maintained information. Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, we decoded the maintained category (tool vs. animal) from 13 MD regions and early visual cortex. Behaviourally, interruption reduced recall accuracy, while the most demanding interrupter slowed responses. Neurally, category information was present during the delay, most strongly in visual cortex and bilateral intraparietal sulcus. This information was unaffected by task engagement (active vs. passive), consistently across decoding accuracy and cross-validated Mahalanobis (crossnobis) distance, with Bayesian evidence supporting the null effect. Increasing the demand of the active interrupter, however, produced a modest, network-wide reduction in crossnobis distance that was not detectable in decoding accuracy. Together, these findings reveal a dissociation between the behavioural costs of interruption and the neural representation of maintained category information. Although interruption impaired recall, engaging in an interrupter did not measurably alter category-level information in the MD network or visual cortex. Increasing the demand of the interrupter produced only a modest, network-wide reduction in representational distance, without affecting decoding accuracy, suggesting that the behavioural costs of interruption may not be fully explained by changes in the categorical representation of the memorandum.

papers.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis Reveals SIRT1-SNCA Correlation in Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects midbrain dopaminergic neurons without any approved therapy. Candidate molecular targets identified in one model are not always traceable across the postmortem, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC), and cell-based systems used to study PD, which complicates clinical translation. To address this gap, we performed an integrative transcriptomic meta-analysis of 33 publicly available datasets across postmortem human brain, iPSC-derived models, and dopaminergic cell lines of PD. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses were combined with STRING protein-protein interaction networks, followed by drug-gene interaction screening against a polyphenol panel. Overall, resveratrol was recovered in all 33 comparisons, independent of model system, tissue, and genetic background. We associated resveratrol with 30 distinct target genes, and SIRT1 was itself a recovered target in 6 comparisons spanning all three model systems. Finally, we resolved the SIRT1-SNCA relationship into four directional patterns that differed by model, inverse in postmortem brain and positive in acutely toxin-exposed cells. These findings support a candidate, context-dependent resveratrol-SIRT1 axis in PD.

papers.title: One digit too many: brain rhythms and autonomic responses at the limits of working memory capacity
papers.abstract: Physiological measures vary with working memory load, but whether they identify when demands exceed a person's working memory capacity remains unclear. We assessed neural and autonomic responses to exceeding digit span by one digit. During an adaptive digit span task, we recorded EEG, pupillometry, and photoplethysmography from 123 participants. We compared each participant's digit span (approximately 70% correct full-sequence recall) with sequences one digit longer (span+1), operationally defined as overload. Full-sequence accuracy decreased from 74.1% to 51.5%, and subjective mental demand increased. Baseline-normalized pulse wave amplitude (PWA) was lower in span+1 from the first digit through terminal retention period. PWA was lower on correctly recalled than erroneous span+1 trials. Phasic pupil responses increased across serial positions but were smaller in span+1 at late span-matched positions; responses did not differ between conditions at their final digits. Non-baseline-corrected pupil diameter was larger in span+1 before sequence onset and during terminal retention, whereas non-baseline-corrected PWA did not differ. Frontal midline theta increased with serial position and was greater during terminal retention in span+1. Alpha and beta power decreased with serial position, and differed between conditions only at late positions. Terminal beta suppression was greater on correctly recalled span+1 trials. Thus, exceeding calibrated span impaired recall without producing a common physiological breakpoint. The findings suggest that reaching this limit does not immediately lead to resource exhaustion or disengagement. Physiological responses showed shifts in timing consistent with adjustments in preparation for recall of the longer sequence, along with increased effort before and during longer sequences.

papers.title: Physical sensorimotor contingencies facilitate learning in monkeys
papers.abstract: Animal studies in neuroscience routinely use virtual tasks that deviate significantly from the animals' natural behavioral repertoire. This choice is often necessary for conducting careful and controlled experimentation. However, this approach raises a fundamental question: do virtual tasks expose neural computations and mechanisms associated with naturalistic tasks? In this study, we explore how naturalistic settings influence learning timescale and generalization behavior in rhesus monkeys. By training animals in a maze-solving task and comparing their behavior across two environments, we observe significant differences. Specifically, we found that a realistic setup using physical objects enabled learning that was orders of magnitude faster than the learning timescale observed in a comparable computerized virtual environment. Furthermore, we noted limited transfer of performance between the physical and virtual settings. These findings underscore the need for understanding how task environments shape learning and generalization, with potential implications for the design of future neuroscience and AI experiments.

papers.title: Differential modulation of the neurocomputational signature of early and late mismatch responses to spoken words by awareness and task relevance
papers.abstract: Mismatch responses (MMRs), including the mismatch negativity (MMN) and the P3, are a hallmark of the brains capacity to detect unexpected events. They are discussed to be generated by two main processes: adaptation and prediction error (PE). However, MMR research on underlying mechanisms has mostly relied on simple, non-linguistic stimuli such as tones, and it remains unknown how awareness and attentional conditions affect MMRs to auditory verbal stimuli, that, unlike tones, carry lexical-semantic meaning. Here, we conducted a preregistered EEG study that disentangled influences of awareness, general task-relevance of word stimuli, and specific target-relevance of word oddballs on the MMN and P3. In addition, single-trial neurocomputational models were applied to uncover the underlying generative models of the MMRs. Results show that word-related MMN and P3 were only elicited when words were task-relevant, and the P3 increased with target-relevance. Crucially, no word-related MMN emerged under inattention, in contrast to the pre-attentive MMN typically reported for tonal deviants. Neurocomputational modeling revealed that the early part of the task-relevant MMN reflects adaptation processes. PE processes generated later parts of the MMN under task-relevance, and the entire MMN under target-relevance, as well as the P3 independent of relevance conditions. This suggests that the same temporal generation pattern of adaptation and PE underlie mismatch responses to both words and tones, but that, unlike tonal MMRs, eliciting MMRs to words requires the allocation of attention. This attentional dependency may reflect the additional lexical-semantic and multi-level representational demands that spoken words impose on the auditory system.

papers.title: Immersion as inference: An active inference account of induced realities and its relation to the two-competitor model
papers.abstract: Immersive technologies are designed for a single target: the human perceptual system. Engineers of virtual and augmented reality have long recognized that a display does not have to replicate the physical world, it only has to provide the inputs that satisfy the senses at the level at which the brain samples them. This engineering intuition is, in fact, a statement about brain function. Here we develop it into a formal account of immersion within the active inference framework. We treat an induced reality (a virtual, augmented, or mixed reality, but also a book or a daydream) as a candidate generative model that competes with the model of the actual reality for the explanation of a shared sensorium and for the control of action. Immersion is then defined as the ensuant belief that the induced reality best explains the current sensory signals and supports the current perceived reality of the winning model, despite any break in immersion by Bayesian model switching driven by a high-precision prediction error that the induced model cannot absorb. Exogenous and endogenous attention, implemented as weights governing stream selection in our earlier two-competitor model, which treated attention as necessary but not sufficient for immersion, appear as two routes of precision allocation: likelihood precision of evolutionarily entrenched sensory events, and precision that follows the expected free energy of policies. Affect and motivation enter through the pragmatic and epistemic value of remaining in the induced reality and through the rate of change of free energy. We show that the two-competitor attentional focus vector and its angle are recovered from the active inference variables, and we reproduce the two scenarios of the original model, a rewarding and a fatiguing activity interrupted by a slamming door, in a minimal simulation. The account links presence, embodiment, cybersickness, and narrative absorption to a single quantity, and it yields concrete predictions for the psychophysiological assessment and closed-loop control of immersion. We discuss implications for neuroergonomic design in which the evolutionarily entrenched core of perception is non-negotiable while its experience-dependent periphery can be trained.

papers.title: Mechanisms of impaired cerebral hemodynamics and memory resilience differ by sex: A role for mineralocorticoid receptors in VCID
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic hypertension is associated with cerebral hypoperfusion and is a primary risk factor for vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID). Aldosterone, a key mediator of hypertension, causes cerebrovascular dysfunction via its mineralocorticoid receptor (MR). METHODS: The effects of MR signaling during hypertension on hemodynamics in two cognition-centric brain regions were determined in both sexes using an established model of VCID (spontaneously hypertensive rat, SHR) and MR antagonist eplerenone. Long-term and spatial working memory were tested, and absolute brain blood flow and brain oxygenation were measured in vivo in CA1 of dorsal hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). RESULTS: Hypertension differentially impaired hemodynamics in a sex- and region-dependent manner. Female SHR had more pervasive hypoperfusion than males that did not affect flow-metabolism coupling. Eplerenone treatment in females restored perfusion in mPFC and hippocampus, improved working memory, but did not protect hippocampal-dependent memory. Eplerenone had no effect in male SHR, indicating the MR-dependent mechanism of VCID is sex-specific. DISCUSSION: This study advances our understanding of how chronic hypertension compromises brain blood flow, suggests that resilience of memory function differs by domain, and that efficacy of interventions depend upon sex.

papers.title: Recruitment of intrasegmental and propriospinal interneuron networks of forelimb motor circuitry in chronic cervical contusion spinal cord injury
papers.abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts descending supraspinal input and spinal networks controlling upper extremity motor function, making recovery of arm and hand function a major priority for affected individuals. The vast majority of regenerative strategies have been studied during the acute and sub-acute phases following SCI, while therapeutic testing remains limited for chronic injury, when persistent barriers significantly limit circuit remodeling. We asked whether pharmacologic enhancement of neuronal-intrinsic axon growth capacity through PTEN inhibition could promote forelimb motor recovery and circuit plasticity in a rodent model of chronic cervical SCI. Following C5 hemi-contusion, female rats underwent behavioral testing of forelimb motor function and received PTEN antagonist peptide (PAP) beginning at a chronic time point, and the trans-synaptic tracer, pseudorabies virus (PRV), was injected into ipsilesional triceps to trace forelimb-associated motor circuitry. PAP selectively improved forelimb usage during cylinder paw-preference testing, but not strength, sensorimotor, or gait-related forelimb measures. PAP increased recruitment of PRV-traced local-projecting and propriospinal interneuron networks. In addition, PAP enhanced synaptic input to these recruited propriospinal interneurons, raising the possibility that spared descending pathways may contribute to recovery through spinal relay circuits. Lastly, we mapped the supraspinal connectome providing descending input from brainstem to the lower motor neurons innervating forelimb muscle, and we determined how this connectome was impacted both by SCI and PAP. Together, these findings show that, even in chronic SCI, pharmacological PTEN inhibition can promote forelimb functional recovery and significant circuit remodeling, with spinal interneuron networks emerging as a key site of PAP-induced plasticity.

papers.title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
papers.abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.

papers.title: Basal ganglia output guides decision-making by state destabilization
papers.abstract: To execute learned behavior, the nervous system can undergo an activity-state transition between the current and the learned activity states. Here, using adult zebrafish, we show that their basal ganglia output induces such state transitions for goal-directed behavior. After learning the Go/No-go task in virtual reality, the striatal indirect pathway responds to negative values of a conditioned cue and the absence of sensory feedback by different neuronal populations. The pallidal output pathway integrates these negative value signals and then broadcasts the integrated signal to the Dc area in the pallium (fish cortex). Optogenetics and mathematical modeling suggested that this pallidal output activity uniformly destabilizes ongoing Dc activity states, thereby facilitating behavioral state transitions toward the behavioral state with the minimum pallidal output activity. This mechanism explains how pallidal output activity guides goal-directed behavior beyond potential barriers between activity states underlying different behavioral states.

papers.title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMS-EEG: The Brain Dynamic Toolbox
papers.abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.

papers.title: Anticipatory Threat of Shock Reduces the Number of Items Reported From a Brief Visual Display: Evidence for Capacity Loss Along the Scanning Order
papers.abstract: Background: Anticipatory anxiety impairs working memory, but whether it also limits the earliest, high-capacity stage of visual storage is unclear. We asked whether the mere expectation of an aversive electrical stimulus reduces how many items people can report from a briefly flashed display, and whether any loss is spatially uniform. Methods: Eighty-eight healthy adults aged 18-25 years were randomly allocated to a threat-of-shock condition (surface electrodes on the wrist and the instruction that a painful stimulus might be delivered; none was) or a control condition (n = 44 each). Participants viewed a 4 x 3 letter matrix for 400 ms and performed untimed written whole report. Correct recall (0-12), intrusions and the position of each reported letter were scored. Groups were compared with Welch's t test, the Mann-Whitney U test, bootstrapped effect sizes, a binomial generalised linear model and a Bayes factor; spatial effects were tested with generalised estimating equations (GEE) accounting for letters nested within participants. Results: The threat group reported fewer correct letters (3.41 +/- 1.09) than controls (4.70 +/- 1.29); Welch t(83.6) = 5.11, p < .001, Hedges' g = 1.08, 95% CI [0.70, 1.53], BF10 ~ 7,549. Intrusions did not differ (p = .376). Recall declined more steeply from left to right under threat (group x column chi2(3) = 11.24, p = .011), with losses confined to the third and fourth letters of the top row (FDR-corrected q <= .003). Conclusions: Anticipatory threat reduced the amount of information transferred from a brief display into a reportable form without increasing guessing. Intact first items and depleted later items along the habitual reading order indicate a reduced number of items read out of a rapidly decaying visual store, rather than a hemifield-specific bias. The single-trial design and the absence of a manipulation check limit mechanistic inference.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods: We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5*5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results: Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 +- 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 +- 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 +- 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion: These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Concurrent metacognitive evaluation is dissociable from perceptual evidence accumulation in the parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires not only accumulating evidence toward a choice but also monitoring its reliability in real time. A central question is whether such concurrent uncertainty is read out directly from the circuit that accumulates perceptual evidence, or is computed by a separate process that runs alongside it. We trained two macaques on a perceptual discrimination task in which they could abandon deliberation at any moment and request assistance, so that uncertainty responses were in parallel with, rather than appended to, evidence accumulation. Behaviorally, a race between distinct perceptual and uncertainty accumulators outperformed models in which the opt-out decision was derived from the perceptual decision variable alone. To ask where the second accumulator resides, we recorded single units in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP), a canonical sensory-motor transformation area, and compared population dynamics with recurrent neural networks instantiating two architectures: one in which uncertainty is computed within the perceptual accumulator, and one in which it is computed outside and triggers the uncertainty response there. LIP exhibited all of these signatures for perceptual choices and none for uncertainty responses. Uncertainty-related activity rose late and stereotypically, lacking the coherence-scaled ramp of an accumulator, and separable from the perceptual accumulation. They are all predicted by the segregated architecture. Concurrent uncertainty is thus represented in LIP but is unlikely to be computed within LIP, indicating that metacognitive monitoring during deliberation is a dissociable operation rather than a derivative readout of the LIP perceptual circuit; its anatomical substrate is not localized here.
